segments.text: Glad you're here for unintended consequences, Episode 25 for June 8, 2026.
Monday, a fresh case to chew on as the week begins. In 2019, a Stanford study examined
what happened after San Francisco expanded rent control in 1994. Landlords removed roughly 15%
of the city's rental stock from the market over the following years. They converted buildings
to condominiums or redevelop them into owner-occupied housing. The policy had been written to keep
working families in their homes. Instead, it accelerated the disappearance of the very apartments
it sought to protect. That outcome matters because it shows how a rule meant to preserve access
can quietly shrink the pool of options for the next wave of residents who never had a unit to begin with.
After World War II, many American and European cities faced acute housing shortages.
Returning veterans and industrial workers competed for limited units.
Local officials watched rents climb sharply in tight markets. They concluded that price
ceilings would prevent displacement and maintain social stability. In New York, the 1943 federal
rent control order and its local successors were defended as temporary measures to protect tenants
from wartime profiteering. In Stockholm, post-war social democratic governments extended wartime
controls into permanent tenant protections. They believed stable rents would let ordinary families
remain in the growing capital. Policy makers in each place treated housing as a necessity,
whose price could be insulated from ordinary supply and demand pressures without long-term damage
to availability. What connects these decisions is the shared assumption that short-term relief
would not reshape the longer-term supply curve, an assumption later data would test directly.
New York system froze rents on pre-1947 buildings and later added rent stabilization for newer stock.
It covered more than 1 million units by the 1970s. San Francisco voters approved rent control in 1979
for buildings built before 1979. They exempted new construction in the hope that fresh supply would
continue to appear. Berlin introduced a five-year rent freeze in 2020 that caped existing leases at
2019 levels for roughly 1.5 million apartments. Early tenant surveys in each city reported
lower eviction filings and greater reported security of tenure. Proponents pointed to these immediate
gains. A minority of economists and housing analysts warned that the caps would discourage maintenance
and new construction. Those cautions rarely altered the political momentum. The pattern is worth noticing
because the visible short-term protection for current tenants often overshadowed the harder to see
effects on future availability. Landlords facing caped revenue responded in predictable ways.
In San Francisco the 1994 expansion prompted many owners to exit the rental market entirely.
The Stanford researchers documented an increase in condo conversions and a measurable decline in
rental housing stock. In stock home, queues for regulated apartments now stretch 8-10 years.
Newcomers are pushed into the unregulated secondary market where rents are often double the
controlled rate. Across cities, owners reduced spending on upkeep once returns were constrained.
This produced visible deterioration in older buildings. Tenants lucky enough to hold controlled
units became less likely to move even when jobs or family needs changed. That reduced labor
mobility and left larger apartments occupied by smaller households. The resulting shortage spilled into
uncontrolled segments. Studies of San Francisco and Cambridge, Massachusetts found that rents in
non-controlled units rose faster than they otherwise would have because overall supply had contracted.
Black market side payments and key money appeared in stock home and New York. These transferred wealth
outside the formal price system the policy had tried to regulate. One implication that surfaces here
is that when supply contracts, the pressure does not vanish. It simply moves to the remaining units
and to informal channels that the original rules never addressed. Cambridge ended rent control
by referendum in 1994. Within four years, average rents informally controlled units rose.
Yet the quantity and quality of rental housing also increased as owners invested again.
New York has repeatedly tightened and loosened its rules. It most recently expanded coverage in 2019
while still confronting chronic shortages. Berlin's 2020 freeze was struck down by the
federal constitutional court in 2021. The city returned to its prior regulatory framework.
No major city has found a durable political path to repeal once controls are in place.
The concentrated benefits to sitting tenants outweigh the diffuse costs to future renters and would
be landlords. Estimates of foregone new construction remain imprecise. The pattern of reduced rental
supply appears consistently across the empirical literature. What stands out in these reversals is how
difficult it becomes to restore balance once sitting tenants have adapted their budgets and expectations
around the controlled price. Price ceilings on a durable good with long production lags tend to shrink
the stock of that good over time. When rules create large windfall gains for current occupants,
those beneficiaries become a durable political constituency that resists later adjustment.
Complex urban housing markets transmit the effects of a single intervention through multiple channels.
Maintenance, conversion, mobility, and new supply are all affected. The net result is rarely confined
to the targeted price. City still weighing similar caps today might first ask what mechanism will ensure
that tomorrow's renters can enter the market at all. Because the evidence from these earlier episodes
shows that the initial protection can quietly reshape who gets to live where for decades afterward.
